data.title: Australia Business Conditions Contract at Fastest Pace in 5 Years
data.description:
By James Glynn

SYDNEY--Australian business conditions contracted at their fastest pace in five years in November, adding to concerns that the economy has slowed sharply following five interest rate rises since the start of 2026.

The headline seasonally adjusted S&P Global Flash Australia PMI composite output index remained below the 50.0 neutral mark for a second consecutive month in November. At 46.1--down from 48.2--the reading was the lowest since August 2021.

The decline was attributed to deeper contractions in output across both the manufacturing and service sectors, with the rates of decline the strongest in 25 and 36 months, respectively.

The Reserve Bank of Australia has raised interest rates aggressively in response to elevated inflation. The official cash rate now stands at 4.85%, its highest level in 18 years.

"November's flash PMI data revealed that Australia's business conditions deteriorated at the sharpest pace in more than five years as the reduction in new orders turned broad-based, with services new business now also in contraction," said Jingyi Pan, economics associate director at S&P Global Market Intelligence.

The PMI data followed last week's release of data showing unemployment jumped in October to 4.9%. Economists expect the RBA to hold rates at its next policy meeting in December.

"The latest decline in demand reflected the impact of higher interest rates, while softening domestic and external conditions also contributed," Pan said.

Inflationary pressures eased for the first time in several months as demand softened across the board, speaking to the effectiveness of the recent tightening of financial conditions, she added.

The data also showed employment fell alongside a marked reduction in business confidence among private-sector firms, pointing to more subdued near-term output conditions at a time when inflation has yet to be fully brought under control, Pan said.

-Write to James Glynn at james.glynn@wsj.com

data.title: Japan Data Preview: Tokyo CPI Expected Up to 16-Month High in November
data.description:
Consensus outlook for Mace News

Friday, November 27, 2026

0830 JST (2330 GMT/1830 EST Thursday, November 26) The Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications releases November Tokyo CPI.

Mace News median: total CPI +3.0% y/y (range: +3.0% to +3.3%) vs. Oct +2.8%; core CPI (ex-fresh food) +2.9% (range: +2.8% to +3.1%) vs. Oct +2.6%; core-core CPI (ex-fresh food, energy) +2.8% (range: +2.7% to +2.9%) vs. Oct +2.6%

TOKYO (MaceNews) - Consumer inflation in Tokyo, a leading indicator of the national trend, is expected to accelerate in all three key readings in November as electricity charges surged after the government ended its summer subsidies at the end of September, having clearer influence on pushing up overall consumer prices.

International oil prices remained elevated amid the unsettled situation in the Middle East. Coupled with the yen’s weakness, higher energy costs were spreading more widely, including through Japanese electricity bills, adding to broad inflationary pressure. Other raw material prices also remained elevated, with import prices staying high amid the weak Japanese currency.

These factors appear to have boosted the core Tokyo consumer price index (CPI), which excludes fresh food, to a 16-month high of 2.9% in November, up from 2.6% in October.

Consumer inflation has started to trend upward as the Tokyo metropolitan government and the central government began scaling back subsidies in recent months. Without fiscal support programs for households, upward price pressures are expected to remain in place.

In addition, there are few signs that this trend will ease, with higher energy, import and labor costs forcing firms in many sectors to raise prices. The conflict in the Middle East continues, while the yen remains weaker than a year earlier, eroding Japan’s purchasing power.

The two other key readings are also expected to accelerate in November, with the total CPI seen reaching 3.0%, its highest level since June 2025, when it stood 3.1%, after rising 2.8% in October. The core-core index, which excludes both fresh food and energy, is expected to rise 2.8% in November, compared with 2.6% a month earlier.

data.title: Zoom faces mounting estimate cuts ahead of Q3 earnings; outlook in focus
data.description:
Zoom Communications is scheduled to report its third-quarter fiscal 2027 results on Monday, November 23, after the market closes. Analysts expect earnings of $1.49 per share on revenue of $1.28B.

Shares fell nearly 15% over the past week, trading 1.19% lower at $82.76 on Friday. The stock initially gained attention following Anthropic's record-breaking stock market debut, but those gains faded during regular trading.

Zoom's exposure to the AI startup through its investment stake has added another factor for investors to watch.

The company also recently made a strategic investment in Medaica through Zoom Ventures to support the expansion of its virtual healthcare platform, which uses connected devices and AI-assisted tools for remote medical examinations. In October, Oppenheimer upgraded Zoom to Outperform from Perform, setting a $130 price target.

However, analyst expectations have weakened ahead of the report. Over the past three months, 17 EPS estimates were revised lower, compared with just two upward revisions. All 22 revenue estimate revisions were downward.

Despite this, Zoom has a relatively strong earnings record, beating EPS estimates in seven of the past eight quarters and revenue estimates in six.

Investors will focus on whether enterprise growth and AI adoption can support revenue momentum. In the previous quarter, revenue increased 4.9% Y/Y to $1.28B, while enterprise revenue grew 7.8% to $787.5M.

For the third quarter, management guided to a revenue of $1.275B–$1.280B and adjusted EPS of $1.46–$1.48.

Profitability and full-year guidance will also be important. Zoom previously forecasted FY27 revenue of $5.085B–$5.095B and adjusted EPS of $6.08–$6.12. Investors will also watch for updates on its Anthropic investment and share repurchases.

Seeking Alpha's ratings are mixed: SA analysts and Wall Street rate the stock buy, with scores of 3.83 and 4.13, respectively, while Quant assigns a Hold rating with a score of 3.18. Profitability remains a key strength, carrying an A+ factor grade, while growth is graded F.

data.title: Bitcoin climbs back above $60K after leveraged longs get flushed
data.description:
Bitcoin spent part of November 20, 2026 doing its best impression of a trapdoor. The world's largest crypto fell to approximately $55,130, its lowest level since at least September 2024, before clawing its way back above $60,000.

The round trip was expensive for anyone holding borrowed bets. Estimates of total liquidations across crypto futures markets ranged from $1.8 billion to $2.7 billion within a 24-hour window, and most of the damage landed on traders who had bet on prices going up.

When prices move far enough against a leveraged position, the exchange automatically closes it to cover the borrowed funds, whether the trader likes it or not.

On this occasion, the forced closures piled up fast. More than $1 billion of liquidations were tied specifically to Bitcoin futures, and the pain was spread across more than 340,000 traders.

Long positions took the majority of the hit. Those are the traders who expected prices to keep rising and borrowed to amplify that view.

Each forced sale pushes prices a little lower, which can trigger the next batch of liquidations. It is a domino effect, and it explains how a decline can accelerate well beyond what ordinary selling would produce.

Then the dominoes ran out. Bitcoin rebounded to around $60,300, a gain of roughly 9% in intraday trading.

On-chain analytics firm Glassnode had flagged the $59,000 to $62,000 range as home to the largest concentration of leveraged long positions. In other words, that band was where a lot of traders were most exposed.

The sell-off tore straight through it. Once those positions were wiped out, the pool of forced sellers waiting below current prices shrank considerably, which eased the immediate downward pressure.

The clearing also helped fuel a short squeeze on the way back up. Short sellers, who profit when prices fall, were caught as the market turned. As they rushed to buy back and close their bets, they added extra fuel to the rebound.

Other major tokens followed Bitcoin higher. Ethereum rose between 3% and 5% during the recovery phase, while Solana gained about 2%.

The liquidation cascade did not happen in a vacuum. US spot Bitcoin ETFs recently posted net outflows of approximately $1.1 billion to $1.5 billion, a sign that some of the money that arrived through traditional brokerage accounts has been heading for the exit.

The outflows lined up with a risk-off mood in technology stocks and broader macroeconomic uncertainty. That context matters because it suggests the drop was not purely a crypto-native leverage problem. Macro nerves and fund outflows set the stage, and overextended futures traders turned a decline into a stampede.

With the biggest cluster of leveraged longs now flushed out of the $59,000 to $62,000 range, the market may be in a somewhat healthier position. Fewer overextended bets sitting just below the price means fewer automatic sell orders waiting to be triggered on the next dip.

For individual traders, the episode is a fresh reminder of how leverage behaves in volatile markets. More than 340,000 traders saw their Bitcoin futures positions closed for them, many at the worst possible moment.

data.title: Japan Week Ahead: Rising Costs, Weak Yen Hurting Households but BOJ Board Seen Leaning Toward Another Rate Hike in December
data.description:
--Government Expected to Keep Modest Economic Recovery Scenario after Q3 GDP Showed Slight Dip due to Stormy Weather, Elevated Inflation

(MaceNews) – In a holiday-shortened week, Japanese data is expected to show inflation is accelerating following a slight contraction in the economy in the July-September quarter caused by sluggish consumer spending amid a temporary factor of bad weather and a continued drag from rising costs.

The economy is expected to post a slight rebound in the October-December quarter, indicating some resilience backed by business investment and exports, but households are cautious about spending in the face of inflation rising toward 3%, well above the Bank of Japan’s 2% target.

Given this outlook, BOJ board members are widely expected to consider a follow-up gradual interest rate hike, a seventh in the current cycle, at their Dec. 17-18 meeting to lift the policy rate further into a more neutral zone and help anchor inflation in the longer term.

In the coming week, board member Naoki Tamura, who has called for raising interest rates sooner than later amid upside risks to inflation, will speak to a business audience. The market focus is also on a speech by Governor Kazuo Ueda on Nov. 30, which is expected to set the tone for the December policy decision along with the findings in the bank’s quarterly Tankan business survey due on Dec. 14.

The latest GDP data released last week showed that Japan’s modest economic recovery stalled in the third quarter, with GDP posting a slight contraction, as stormy weather and rising costs dampened private consumption and net exports slipped back, offsetting a solid rebound in business investment. Public works spending continued to fall amid fading effects of the fiscal 2025 supplementary budget and labor shortages.

The gross domestic product fell 0.02% on quarter, or an annualized 0.1%, marking its first contraction in four quarters after growing 0.4% or an upwardly revised 1.7% annualized in Q2. The domestic demand added 0.6 percentage point to the total domestic output while net exports trimmed 0.6 point after pushing up the economy by 0.6 point in Q2, when imports plunged due to squeezed crude oil shipments from the war-hit Mideast Gulf.

The headline figures came in weaker than the median economist forecast of +0.1% on quarter or +0.3% annualized but was still above the low end of the forecast range at -0.1% (-0.3% annualized).

The consumer price index data for Tokyo, a leading indicator of the national trend, is forecast to have accelerated in November as many firms continued passing higher import, material and labor costs. The core measure (excluding fresh food) is forecast to post a 2.9% increase on year, a 16-month high, after easing to 2.6% in October.

This follows the release last week of the more comprehensive national average CPI. Consumer inflation in October stayed relatively high after accelerating to just above the BOJ 2% price stability target in September. An end to the metropolitan government’s water subsidies for the peak summer months led to a rise in overall energy prices after falling in recent months. The annual rate in consumer prices also edged up in October as the weak yen and global memory chip shortages pushed up the prices for mobile phones while strong demand from visitors from overseas lifted accommodations costs.

The year-on-year increase in the core CPI edged up to a 10-month high of 2.2% in October after rising to 2.1% in September and unexpectedly easing to 1.7% in August. The national average CPI has been tamer than the Tokyo area data but economists expect it to move up toward 3% in coming months.

Monday, Nov. 23

- Japanese markets are closed for the Labor Thanksgiving Day public holiday.

Tuesday, Nov. 24

c. 1715 JST (0815 GMT/0315 EST Tuesday, Nov. 24) The Cabinet Office releases the government’s monthly economic report for November.

The government is expected to maintain its overview that the economy is “recovering at a moderate pace” and that the moderate recovery will continue in the near term. It is also likely to repeat its warning about rising costs under the protracted Iran war and the depressed value of the Japanese currency, the latter of which has kept imports expensive.

In its monthly report for October released last month, the government stuck to its long-held view that the economy was “recovering at a moderate pace but the impact of the situation in the Middle East needs a close attention.” The government also repeated the need to keep a close watch on “fluctuations in the financial and capital markets.” Bond yields have risen this year over fears of large fiscal spending and elevated inflation while the yen remains weak.

Thursday, Nov. 26

1000 JST (0100 GMT Thursday/2100 EST Wednesday, Nov. 25) Bank of Japan board member Naoki Tamura, formerly with the SMBC financial group, speaks to business leaders in the central Japan prefecture of Yamanashi. He and his colleague Hajime Takata, who came from Mizuho Securities, have called for raising interest rates sooner than later, noting upside risks to inflation.

Friday, Nov. 27

0830 JST (2330 GMT/1830 EST Thursday, Nov. 26) The Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications releases November Tokyo CPI.

Mace News median: total CPI +3.0% y/y (range: +3.0% to +3.3%) vs. Oct +2.8%; core CPI (ex-fresh food) +2.9% (range: +2.8% to +3.1%) vs. Oct +2.6%; core-core CPI (ex-fresh food, energy) +2.8% (range: +2.7% to +2.9%) vs. Oct +2.6%

Consumer inflation in Tokyo, a leading indicator of the national trend, is forecast to have accelerated in November as many firms continued passing higher import, material and labor costs. An end to the metropolitan government’s water subsidies for the peak summer months had turned year-on-year drops in overall energy prices into an increase by October. Nationwide subsidies for fuels are still keeping energy prices below year-earlier levels but households are expected to be hit by the widespread move among firms to raise sales prices.

All three key CPI measures are well above the Bank of Japan’s 2% price stability target. Without the effects of fiscal support programs for households, inflation is expected to stay elevated for now. The Mideast conflict lingers, keeping energy costs high, while the yen remains under year-earlier levels, eroding Japan’s purchasing power.

The core measure (excluding fresh food) is forecast to post a 2.9% increase on year, a 16-month high, after easing to 2.6% in October and surging to a 10-month high of 2.7% in September. The core rate hit a recent peak at 3.6% in May 2025 when processed food price hikes were sharp in the aftermath of domestic rice shortages.

The annual rate of the total CPI is also expected to rise to a 16-month high of 3.0% after inching up to 2.8% in October from 2.7% in September. The year-on-year increase in the core-core CPI (excluding fresh food and energy), which is not directly impacted by fuel and utility subsidies, is seen at 2.8% after slowing to 2.6% in October and jumping to a 13-month high of 2.9% in the prior month.

At its Oct. 29-30 meeting, the BOJ’s nine-member board decided to leave the target for the overnight interest rate at 1.25% in an 8 to 1 vote as officials assessed the cumulative effects of the six rate hikes conducted since April 2024 as part of the normalization of large-scale easing. Governor Kazuo Ueda told a post-meeting news conference that there is still room for the rate to be raised to be comfortably into a range of 1.1% to 2.5% that is considered neutral to economic activity. Barring a spike in uncertainty over geopolitical risks, the bank is widely expected to follow up with another 25-basis point rate hike in December or January.

Board members now believe that underlying inflation is “at a level that is generally consistent” with the bank’s 2% price stability target, instead of “nearing” the level as stated until the previous meeting. The board continues to describe financial conditions as “accommodative,” another reason for the need to raise interest rates further.
